question: Early golf balls were completely smooth, but today every golf ball is covered in small dimples. Why?
correct_answer: Less air drag, so it flies farther
alternative_answers: To make it fly straighter and longer
headline_answer: Less air drag, so it flies farther
source_excerpt: dimples reduce drag on a sphere as much as 50% as compared to a smooth surface

extra.verification_notes: Dimples trigger a turbulent boundary layer that delays separation and cuts drag (up to ~50%), so the ball flies farther; see Choi et al. 2006.

explanation: Golfers noticed that old, scuffed and battered balls flew farther than new smooth ones, so manufacturers began adding a pattern to the surface on purpose. The dimples create a thin layer of turbulent air that clings to the ball's surface. That shrinks the low-pressure wake behind the ball, which sharply reduces drag. With backspin, the dimples also help generate lift. Together these effects let a dimpled ball travel roughly twice as far as an identical smooth one.

question: On which planet does a single rotation, one full day, take longer than an entire orbit of the Sun?
source_excerpt: Venusian sidereal day, 243 Earth days, lasts longer than a Venusian year, 224.7 Earth days.

extra.why_interesting: A day being longer than a year sounds impossible. The player can still reason toward a slow-spinning neighbour.
extra.verification_notes: Venus's sidereal rotation (243 d) exceeds its orbital period (224.7 d); no other planet does this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus).

explanation: Venus spins once every 243 Earth days but circles the Sun in about 225. It also spins backwards, so there the Sun rises in the west.

question: The Eiffel Tower is measurably taller on a hot summer day than in winter. What causes this growth?
source_excerpt: The tower also grows about 15 cm (6 in) taller during the summer, due to thermal expansion of the iron.

extra.why_interesting: Players think of a monument as fixed. A building that 'grows' each summer is surprising, yet everyday physics gets you there.
extra.verification_notes: Thermal expansion of the iron is the accepted cause of the tower's summer growth (up to ~15 cm); no newer developments contradict it, though I did not open the cited page this session.

explanation: Its 7,000-plus tonnes of iron expand in the heat. That lifts the tip by up to about 15 centimetres.

question: Which is the only nation to have played at every men's FIFA World Cup finals tournament since 1930?
source_excerpt: Brazil, the only nation to appear in every World Cup, now sit third in the South American standings, guaranteeing a top-six finish.

extra.why_interesting: Many players will guess it quickly, but some will hesitate between Brazil, Germany and Italy, which missed tournaments.

topicality.rationale: Long-standing football record, not tied to a recent event.

extra.verification_notes: Brazil is the only nation to have appeared in every men's World Cup, and it qualified for the 2026 edition, extending the streak (https://www.freemalaysiatoday.com/category/sports/2025/06/11/brazil-qualify-for-2026-world-cup-finals).

explanation: Germany and Italy each missed tournaments, so Brazil is the only ever-present. It has also won the trophy a record five times.

question: The 'Fosbury Flop', clearing the bar backwards and head-first, revolutionised which athletics event after the 1968 Olympics?
source_excerpt: The Fosbury flop is a technique for the high jump event in track and field... became the dominant style of the event.

extra.why_interesting: The description of the technique alone lets a player picture the event and reason their way to it.
extra.verification_notes: The Fosbury Flop is a high jump technique that became dominant after Fosbury's 1968 Olympic gold (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fosbury_Flop).

explanation: Dick Fosbury won gold in Mexico City with it, and within a decade almost every elite jumper had copied him.

question: Outside Japan, most of the green 'wasabi' served with sushi is actually mainly which other pungent root, dyed green?
source_excerpt: most commercial wasabi is made from horseradish and other ingredients

extra.why_interesting: Sushi lovers believe they have eaten wasabi many times. Most have not, and the culprit is a root they already know.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple sources, including Food Network, confirm that most 'wasabi' outside Japan is horseradish (often with mustard) dyed green.

explanation: Real wasabi is expensive and notoriously hard to grow. Restaurants usually serve horseradish paste with mustard and green colouring instead.

question: The world's most expensive spice by weight is hand-picked as three tiny red threads from the centre of which purple flower?
source_excerpt: Each flower's three-pronged style ends in a crimson stigma; premium saffron regularly exceeds US$5,000 per kilogram.

extra.why_interesting: People know saffron is expensive but rarely know it comes from a common garden flower.
extra.verification_notes: Saffron, from the purple Crocus sativus flower, has three hand-picked crimson stigmas per flower and is widely regarded as the costliest spice by weight; I found no contradiction.

explanation: Saffron is the stigmas of the saffron crocus. It takes well over a hundred thousand flowers to make a single kilogram.

question: Counting all its overseas territories, which country covers more time zones than any other, twelve in total?
source_excerpt: Owing to the number of territories it governs beyond Europe, France has 12 (and for a period of the year 13) time zones.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone reaches for Russia or the USA. The 'overseas territories' foothold lets a sharp player pivot to France.
extra.verification_notes: Guinness World Records credits France with the most time zones (12, or 13 for part of the year) thanks to its overseas territories; Russia and the US have 11.

explanation: From French Polynesia in the Pacific to Réunion in the Indian Ocean, France outspans both Russia and the United States.

question: Which Siberian lake, the deepest on Earth, holds roughly a fifth of the planet's unfrozen surface fresh water?
source_excerpt: It is estimated that the lake contains around 19% of the unfrozen fresh water on the planet.

extra.why_interesting: One lake holding a fifth of Earth's liquid surface fresh water is startling. 'Siberian' and 'deepest' give a fair path to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: Baikal is the deepest lake (1,642 m) and holds about 19% of unfrozen fresh water, which is roughly a fifth; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal

explanation: Baikal is over 1,600 metres deep and around 25 million years old, which makes it the oldest lake on the planet too.

question: After his defeat at Waterloo, Napoleon was exiled to which remote South Atlantic island, where he died in 1821?
source_excerpt: He died at Longwood, on the Atlantic island of Saint Helena, where he had been exiled following his defeat at the battle of Waterloo.

extra.why_interesting: Many players remember Elba and will be tempted by it. The 'South Atlantic' clue rewards those who know there was a second exile.
extra.verification_notes: Napoleon was exiled to Saint Helena after Waterloo and died there on 5 May 1821, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Napoleon.

explanation: He had already escaped once from Elba in the Mediterranean, so the British chose an island nearly 2,000 kilometres off the African coast.

question: In which year did Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first stand on the summit of Mount Everest?
source_excerpt: On 29 May, four days before the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, the chosen pair reached the 8848-m summit of Mt Everest via the south-east ridge.

extra.why_interesting: Players often place the conquest of Everest later than it was, in the space-race era. The coronation link gives a satisfying anchor.
extra.verification_notes: Hillary and Tenzing summited Everest on 29 May 1953, so 1953 is correct; no newer event can change this (https://nzhistory.govt.nz/edmund-hillary-and-tensing-norgay-reach-summit-of-everest).

explanation: They summited on 29 May 1953, and the news reached London on the eve of Queen Elizabeth the Second's coronation.

question: Who remains the only person ever to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences?
source_excerpt: Marie Curie was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911.

extra.why_interesting: Many know Curie as a Nobel winner. Fewer realise her double in two different sciences has never been repeated.
extra.verification_notes: Marie Curie won Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911) and is still the only person with Nobels in two different sciences; the 2026 Physics laureate (Halzen) is not a prior laureate, and the 2026 Chemistry laureate was not found.

explanation: She won Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911. She was also the first woman to win a Nobel Prize at all.

question: How many hearts does an octopus have?
source_excerpt: An octopus has three hearts: a systemic heart and two branchial hearts, each attached to one of the two gills.

extra.why_interesting: One heart is the default assumption, so any number above it is a delight. Some players half-remember the answer.
extra.verification_notes: Octopuses have three hearts (one systemic, two branchial), per Live Science (https://www.livescience.com/how-many-hearts-does-an-octopus-have).

explanation: Two hearts push blood through the gills and the third serves the body. That blood is blue, thanks to a copper-based protein.

question: True or false: bulls charge at a matador's cape because the colour red enrages them.
source_excerpt: bulls charge either colour just as readily as they do the red muleta, and it is motion that provokes the bull's charge

extra.why_interesting: 'Red rag to a bull' is a near-universal belief. Busting it gives a satisfying reversal.
extra.verification_notes: Cattle are red-green colour-blind and charge at the cape's movement, not its colour, so the myth is false (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muleta).

explanation: Bulls can't really tell red from green. It is the cape's sweeping movement that provokes the charge, and they'd go for a blue one just the same.

question: Roughly how far away is the Moon from Earth?
source_excerpt: the average distance between the blue planet and its only natural satellite is about 238,855 miles (384,400 kilometers)

extra.why_interesting: Diagrams squash the Moon close to Earth, so players badly underestimate the gap. The planets-in-the-gap payoff makes the scale stick.
extra.verification_notes: The Moon's mean distance is about 384,400 km, so 'About 400,000 km' is the only reasonable option, per https://space.com/18145-how-far-is-the-moon.html.

explanation: On average it is about 384,000 kilometres away. That is so far that all the other planets of the solar system could line up side by side in the gap.

question: Bananas are very slightly radioactive. Which element they are famously rich in is responsible?
source_excerpt: The banana equivalent dose is a way of expressing the amount of radiation in terms of the radiation from eating one banana, from potassium-40.

extra.why_interesting: A radioactive fruit sounds alarming. The answer is the nutrient bananas are famous for, so the player can get there.
extra.verification_notes: Bananas' slight radioactivity comes from potassium-40, as described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana_equivalent_dose; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: A tiny share of all potassium is radioactive potassium-40. Physicists even joke about the 'banana equivalent dose', and it's entirely harmless.

question: Three of these countries are landlocked. Which one has a sea coast?
source_excerpt: South America has only two landlocked countries

extra.why_interesting: Paraguay and Uruguay are constantly confused, and Bolivia once had a coast, so the player must genuinely know their maps.
extra.verification_notes: Paraguay, Bolivia and Mongolia are landlocked while Uruguay has an Atlantic/Río de la Plata coast; South America has only two landlocked countries (https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/landlocked-countries-of-the-world.html).

explanation: Uruguay faces the Atlantic. Bolivia did have a coastline, until it lost it to Chile in the War of the Pacific in the 1880s.

question: The shoreline of which salt lake is the lowest point on dry land anywhere on Earth?
source_excerpt: its shores are the lowest land-based elevation on Earth

extra.why_interesting: An approachable record. 'Salt lake' and 'lowest' point most players straight to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: The Dead Sea's shore is the lowest land-based elevation on Earth (about -440 m, still falling), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea; no newer development changes this.

explanation: Its shores lie more than 430 metres below sea level, and the water level is still dropping by about a metre a year.

question: Because Earth bulges at the equator, the point on land farthest from Earth's centre isn't Everest's summit but a volcano's peak in which country?
source_excerpt: widely reported to be the farthest point on the surface from Earth's center

extra.why_interesting: 'Highest' always means Everest, until you measure from the centre of the Earth. The equator hint lets a sharp player land on Ecuador.
extra.verification_notes: Chimborazo (Ecuador) is widely reported as the point on Earth's surface farthest from the centre, with Huascarán in Peru a close runner-up; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimborazo

explanation: The summit of Chimborazo sits about two kilometres farther from Earth's core than Everest's, even though it is far lower above sea level.

question: True or false: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the first Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
source_excerpt: Cleopatra was born about 2,500 years after the Great Pyramid was finished, and the Moon landing came about 2,000 years after her birth.

extra.why_interesting: Players lump all of ancient Egypt into one era. The sheer length of Egyptian history makes Cleopatra closer to us than to the pyramid builders.
extra.verification_notes: Cleopatra (69–30 BC) lived about 2,000 years before the 1969 Moon landing but about 2,500 years after the Great Pyramid (c. 2560 BC), so True is correct (https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/so-cleopatra-lived-closer-in-time-to-the-first-lunar-landing-than-the-great-pyramids.html).

explanation: The Great Pyramid was about 2,500 years old by Cleopatra's time, while barely 2,000 years separate her from Apollo 11.

question: The Rosetta Stone repeats one decree in hieroglyphs, in Demotic script, and in which language scholars could already read, the key to cracking the code?
source_excerpt: Scholars could read the Ancient Greek, which was widely known to them and gave them their starting point.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the stone cracked hieroglyphs but not how. The answer is the one language scholars could already read, which logic can reach.
extra.verification_notes: The Rosetta Stone has hieroglyphic, Demotic and Ancient Greek texts, and scholars could already read the Greek (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosetta_Stone).

explanation: By comparing the Greek with the hieroglyphs, Jean-François Champollion finally deciphered Egyptian writing in 1822.

question: Despite its Roman-sounding name, the Caesar salad was invented in the 1920s in which Mexican city, just south of San Diego?
source_excerpt: The salad was created on July 4, 1924, at Caesar's restaurant in Tijuana, Mexico, during a holiday rush that depleted the kitchen's supplies.

extra.why_interesting: The name screams ancient Rome, but the truth is a 1920s Mexican border town. 'Just south of San Diego' gives a fair path.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Caesar salad was created in 1924 at Caesar's restaurant in Tijuana; the disputes are over who made it, not where.

explanation: Italian-born restaurateur Caesar Cardini created it there, serving Americans who crossed the border to escape Prohibition.

question: With which song did ABBA win the Eurovision Song Contest in 1974?
source_excerpt: Sweden won with "Waterloo," performed by ABBA. It was Sweden's first contest win.

extra.why_interesting: A cheerful, gettable pop moment that most international adults can sing along to.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms ABBA won Eurovision 1974 with 'Waterloo' for Sweden; no disqualification or later change to the result was found.

explanation: Their win in Brighton launched Sweden's biggest pop export onto a global career of hits.

question: Released in 1995, what was the first feature-length film made entirely with computer animation?
source_excerpt: Toy Story was the first feature-length computer-animated film and the first theatrical film produced by Pixar.

extra.why_interesting: Easy and nostalgic. The year and 'computer animation' clue most players in quickly.
extra.verification_notes: Toy Story (1995) is widely credited as the first entirely computer-animated feature film; no contradicting or newer claim found.

explanation: Pixar's tale of Woody and Buzz Lightyear changed animation for good and kicked off a franchise still going decades later.

question: Queen frontman Freddie Mercury was born Farrokh Bulsara in 1946 on which island off the coast of East Africa?
source_excerpt: born on 5 September 1946 in Stone Town, in the British protectorate of Zanzibar, East Africa

extra.why_interesting: Mercury feels quintessentially British rock. His East African island birthplace surprises, and the clue narrows it to a few candidates.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Mercury was born in 1946 in Stone Town, Zanzibar (main island Unguja, commonly called Zanzibar Island); nothing newer contradicts it.

explanation: He grew up between Zanzibar and India. His family fled to England after the 1964 revolution on the island.

question: In the 1939 film 'The Wizard of Oz', Dorothy's magic slippers are ruby red. What colour were they in the original book?
source_excerpt: The 1900 book describes them as silver, and the ruby-red version was an invention of the 1939 MGM adaptation.

extra.why_interesting: The ruby slippers are iconic, so learning they were invented for the film is a delight. A metal colour is a reasonable guess.
extra.verification_notes: In Baum's 1900 novel Dorothy's magic shoes are silver; the ruby colour was introduced by the 1939 MGM film (https://www.fatherly.com/news/everything-need-to-know-about-dorothys-ruby-slippers-wizard-oz-silver/).

explanation: The filmmakers switched to ruby to show off the new Technicolor process, and the red version became cinema legend.

question: Before he was called Mario, Nintendo's famous hero made his debut in the 1981 arcade game 'Donkey Kong' under what name?
source_excerpt: Mario was first called "Ossan" by the development team behind the original Donkey Kong... called "Jumpman" in the English instructions.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows Mario, and few know his first name. What he did in that game is a strong foothold for a proud guess.
extra.verification_notes: Mario debuted in Donkey Kong (1981) as 'Jumpman' in the English instructions; 'Ossan' was only an internal nickname (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario).

explanation: He was a carpenter rather than a plumber back then. Reportedly he was renamed after the landlord of Nintendo's American warehouse, Mario Segale.

question: The Rubik's Cube was invented in 1974 by an architecture professor in which country?
source_excerpt: Ernő Rubik, a Hungarian sculptor, invented the puzzle in 1974 in Hungary.

extra.why_interesting: A world-famous toy with an unexpected Central European origin. Many players half-know it, and the name's sound is a subtle foothold.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Ernő Rubik, a Hungarian professor of architecture, invented the cube in 1974 in Hungary.

explanation: Ernő Rubik built it in Budapest as a teaching tool and called it the 'Magic Cube'. It went on to become one of the best-selling toys ever.

question: The marathon's oddly precise distance of 42.195 kilometres was set so the race at which city's Olympics could finish in front of the royal box?
source_excerpt: a lap of the track that ended in front of the Royal Box

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the odd distance comes from ancient Greece. It actually exists for a royal finish line, and 'royal box' points toward London.
extra.verification_notes: The 42.195 km distance derives from the 1908 London Olympics course, which ended in front of the royal box at White City Stadium (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon).

explanation: At the 1908 Games the course ran from Windsor Castle to the stadium's royal box, and that distance was later made the official standard.
